title: The Vow at the Poisoned Lake
story:
One morning Krishna went into the forest alone — not with Balarama, his brother, and not with the cowherd boys who usually followed at his heels. Only himself: dark as a rain cloud, a feather in his hair, garlands of fresh kadamba and arjuna blossoms around his neck, and a flute in his hand, walking wherever the cattle led him. The woods of Vrindavan that day seemed made for wandering. Peacocks called from the branches, and low thunder muttered among the hills, as if the season itself leaned close to listen.

He had ranged here before, and the forest always answered him. Plantain groves stood thick and green, the ground was soft with new grass and studded with lotuses, and the air carried the scent of dark-blue lotus from the water. Fountains lay hidden among the trees, and the wind that came off the leaves fanned him as he walked. Sometimes he would stop beneath the great Bhandiraka fig tree, tall enough to seem to brush the sky, its branches bowed with fruit, and let the cowherd boys amuse him with their songs, answering them, note for note, on his flute. It was the kind of place, the old verses say, where a boy might sing to his cows and believe the whole earth was listening.

Then one day, while the cattle grazed and the sun climbed higher, he came down to the bank of the Yamuna. The river lay before him like a woman dressed for a festival — lilies and lotuses on her water, swans and cranes calling over it, landing-stairs worn smooth, a current strong and sweet, her little lakes catching the light, and waterfowl ranging over her in pairs. It should have been the sweetest water in the world.

But the river was not well. There, in a lake along her side, lived Kaliya, the serpent-king, and his venom had seeped into the water until it was no longer fit to drink. Nothing that drank from it could live. The birds had gone quiet over the pool, and for all its beauty the water carried a hidden bitterness that could kill.

Krishna stood at the water's edge and looked into the deep. He did not rage, and he did not turn away. Quietly, the way a boy decides to climb a tree for its fruit, he made up his mind. "I should vanquish this king of serpents," he resolved. "I shall climb the kadamba tree, jump into the lake, and vanquish Kaliya."

It was such a small sentence for so great a deed, and he spoke it without raising his voice. But the resolve was set, and the water, as if it knew, seemed to darken under his gaze.
reflection: The striking thing about the resolve is its quiet. Krishna does not rehearse a battle or boast of strength; he decides the way a boy decides to climb a tree, and the whole deliverance of the river hangs on that calm sentence.
tradition_note: This moment of resolve is particular to the Harivamsha; the Bhagavata Purana moves more directly from the poisoning of the river to the leap.
next_story_tease: But the poisoned water had already begun its silent work on the unsuspecting cowherds and their cattle.
hero_scene: Krishna standing alone at the edge of the poisoned lake, flute lowered in his hand, gazing into the dark water as the great kadamba tree rises behind him.
visual_elements: Krishna with a feather in his hair
